title: The Bell of Vessel Farm
premise: Folklorist August Yarrow arrives at Vessel Farm to record the last living singer of a village whose church bell was melted down in 1911 — only to hear it ring at midnight from an empty tower. The bell, it turns out, was never destroyed but buried, and it counts: each ring claims a member of the family that sold it. August, an estranged cousin by blood they never knew they had, must learn the song the village refuses to sing twice — the only thing that can silence the count — before it finishes ringing. In the end August sings it themselves at the cost of their own name and memory, becoming the farm's next keeper while the family walks free.
about_author: Mirabel Blackwood grew up in a farming village on the Welsh marches where, she insists, the church clock has been stopped at the same minute since before anyone living was born. She writes horror from a farmhouse she refuses to leave after dark.

chapters.title: Songs Sung Once
chapters.summary: August Yarrow, POV: arrives in the village of Hollowmere to record folk songs for an archive, armed with a tape recorder and cheerful skepticism. The innkeeper warns them never to ask anyone to sing the same song twice. Emotional beat: wry confidence curdling into first unease.

chapters.title: The Vessel Inheritance
chapters.summary: POV August: August travels to Vessel Farm, recently left to a family they've never met — the Vessels, who turn out to share a great-grandmother with August. The matriarch, Edith, is coldly welcoming. Emotional beat: awkward kinship, a house that watches back.

chapters.title: Nineteen Eleven
chapters.summary: POV August, with Edith's reluctant testimony: the church bell was melted down in 1911 after the Vessels of that era sold it to pay a debt. Edith insists the metal never left the parish. August finds the parish ledger's bell page torn out. Emotional beat: curiosity hardening into obsession.

chapters.title: What the Well Kept
chapters.summary: POV August: exploring the farm, August finds a sealed well and, at its lip, a rope worn smooth by generations of hands. A child's rhyme about 'the count' is chalked inside the barn. Emotional beat: dread arriving ahead of explanation.

chapters.title: The First Ring
chapters.summary: POV August: at midnight the church tower — empty since 1911 — rings once. Every villager shuts their windows. Edith goes grey and begins packing. Emotional beat: the moment belief is no longer optional, and August still refuses.

chapters.title: The Village That Won't Say
chapters.summary: POV August: August canvasses villagers; each recorded song, played back, is missing its second verse. An old man, Tam, nearly speaks, then bites his tongue bloody. Emotional beat: a wall of complicit silence, and August's recorder as an instrument of intrusion.

chapters.title: Blood in the Ledger
chapters.summary: POV August: in the parish records August discovers the 1911 sale was signed by a Vessel using blood, not ink, and that every signer's line has since died 'in the count.' August's own name appears in a later hand. Emotional beat: inheritance revealed as debt.

chapters.title: One
chapters.summary: POV Edith: the bell rings a second time; Edith's brother dies in his sleep, smiling. The family understands: the bell counts down the Vessel line. Edith orders the children sent away. Emotional beat: grief braided with terrible arithmetic.

chapters.title: The Song Twice
chapters.summary: POV August: August finally hears the full song — from the well, at midnight, in a voice that is almost their grandmother's. The second verse is a bargain: sing it back to the bell, and it stops — but the singer must 'stay for the count.' Emotional beat: temptation and refusal.

chapters.title: Two
chapters.summary: POV Edith: a second death, and the village begins treating the Vessels as already dead — shopkeepers refuse their money. Edith confesses to August that the family once tried to flee in 1943; the road simply returned them. Emotional beat: claustrophobia of a trap with no outside.

chapters.title: The Melted Bell
chapters.summary: POV August: August finds the 1911 'melted' bell in the well, whole and green with age, and realizes the melt was staged — the village hid it and let the family take the curse. Emotional beat: betrayal; the horror has human authors.

chapters.title: Tam's Tongue
chapters.summary: POV Tam: the old bell-ringer's apprentice breaks and tells August the ritual's rules — the song must be sung by blood at the bell's mouth, and the bell must be answered, not silenced. He dies before finishing, his mouth full of river water though he's nowhere near the river. Emotional beat: the cost of speech.

chapters.title: Three
chapters.summary: POV August: the third ring takes Edith's daughter-in-law. The surviving Vessels turn on August — the outsider whose name is in the ledger — blaming their blood for waking the bell. Emotional beat: family fracturing; August's identity as kin and stranger at once.

chapters.title: What August Forgot
chapters.summary: POV August: digging into their own childhood, August recalls a lullaby their grandmother sang — the same song, second verse intact. August has known it all along; the archive work was a return, not a discovery. Emotional beat: the self as haunted house.

chapters.title: The Road That Returns
chapters.summary: POV Edith: the family attempts flight again, loading a truck at dawn. Milestones repeat; they arrive back at their own gate as the sun sets. The youngest child begins humming the bell's note. Emotional beat: despair perfected.

chapters.title: Four
chapters.summary: POV August: the fourth ring claims Edith's son. Only Edith, the children, and August remain. August decides to sing, and Edith — who has known August's name was in the ledger all along — finally admits she invited them as a sacrifice. Emotional beat: betrayal and resolve colliding.

chapters.title: The Well, Opened
chapters.summary: POV August: August and Edith's granddaughter lower the bell from the well together; inside its crown, names are scratched — one added per ring. August's is already there, older than their birth. Emotional beat: fatalism faced head-on.

chapters.title: The Count
chapters.summary: POV August: at midnight August climbs the tower and sings the second verse to the bell as it swings itself. The counting falters; the village, drawn into the street for the first time, watches. Emotional beat: the climax — one voice against a century of silence.

chapters.title: Five
chapters.summary: POV Edith: the bell rings a fifth time — for August. August's name fades from their own memory even as the children's names vanish from the bell's crown. Edith holds August's recorder, the only proof August existed. Emotional beat: sacrifice completed, grief without a grave.

chapters.title: The New Keeper
chapters.summary: POV Edith: the bell falls silent; the village slowly unclenches. August remains at Vessel Farm, courteous and blank, tending the well, unable to leave — the road now returns them, too. Emotional beat: survival's price made domestic.

chapters.title: The Archive Recording
chapters.summary: POV Edith's granddaughter, years later: she donates August's tapes to the folk archive. Played back, every song is complete — except the last track, where a voice that isn't quite August's sings the second verse, and asks to be sung to. Emotional beat: haunting as inheritance.

chapters.title: The Bell of Vessel Farm
chapters.summary: POV the granddaughter: she brings her own child to the farm, and the new keeper — August's face, someone else's patience — teaches the girl the lullaby. When the girl sings it back, the well rope creaks, satisfied. Emotional beat: the cycle accepted, the price paid forward.
